bites.title: Usage reviews and expansion opportunities
bites.body:
Before a contract comes up for renewal, review how staff are actually using the system each week and where adjacent bottlenecks have appeared. High adoption and requests for extra features are natural signals to propose a well-scoped phase two.

If a recruitment firm's consultants use your CV summary bot fifty times a day and start asking whether it can also draft candidate outreach emails, you have a proven expansion opportunity.

Conversely, if usage has quietly dropped off, investigate why and fix the friction in the current workflow before trying to sell anything new.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: What should a consultant do if a usage review shows that client staff have stopped using the current bot?

choices.text: Immediately try to sell the client a much larger and more expensive second bot team
Find out what friction caused usage to drop and fix the existing workflow before pitching new features
Ignore the drop in usage and hope the client renews the contract without checking
Blame the staff in a formal email to the company owner without speaking to the team

questions.explanation: Fixing adoption friction in the current tool restores value and earns the right to propose future expansions.

bites.title: Quarterly check on whether the goal has shifted
bites.body:
Small businesses change direction quickly as seasons, suppliers, and markets shift, so hold a quarterly review with the client owner to check whether the bot system is still aiming at the right business goal. A system that brilliantly solves last year's problem can become irrelevant if the business has moved on.

A garden centre might need their bot team focused on delivery tracking during the spring rush, but want the focus shifted to trade account queries and winter workshops by autumn.

Adjusting priorities every quarter keeps your retainer tied to the owner's top current concern rather than becoming a forgotten background expense.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Why is a quarterly goal review with the client important even when the bots are running without errors?

choices.text: Language models automatically erase their system prompts at the end of every calendar quarter
Quarterly meetings are the only time a consultant is allowed to check error logs
A client's business priorities shift over time, and the system must stay aligned with what matters now
It gives the consultant an excuse to rewrite the entire codebase every ninety days

questions.explanation: Regular strategic check-ins ensure the automation adapts as the client's seasonal and commercial priorities evolve.

bites.title: Ask what to stop doing as well as what to add
bites.body:
During reviews, always ask which bot features, reports, or approval steps are no longer earning their keep and can be switched off. Removing unused steps simplifies maintenance, cuts token bills, and keeps the staff interface uncluttered.

It is like pruning a fruit tree in winter: cutting back dead or crowded branches gives the healthy branches room to produce better fruit next season.

When a client sees you proactively retiring a bot step to save them money and screen clutter, they trust that your recommendations to add new capabilities are genuine.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Why should you ask a client what to remove or stop doing during a system review?

choices.text: Pruning unused features lowers cost and complexity, and proves you care about efficiency rather than just upselling
Removing features is the only way to increase your monthly consulting invoice
Bots cannot function if a team has more than two features turned on at once
It allows you to delete the client's security controls and audit logs to save time

questions.explanation: Proactively retiring low-value steps keeps the system lean and builds deep trust when you do recommend worthwhile additions.

bites.title: Referrals and case studies, with client permission
bites.body:
Happy clients with proven ROI are the strongest source of new consulting work through referrals and short case studies. Once you have delivered clear, measured results, ask the client whether they would be willing to share a brief testimonial or introduce you to another business owner.

A one-page case study showing how a local logistics firm cut invoice processing time by seventy per cent, backed by a quote from their managing director, wins trust faster than any cold pitch.

Always get explicit written permission before naming a client or sharing any numbers publicly, or offer an anonymised case study if they prefer to keep their competitive edge private.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: What must a consultant always do before publishing a case study about a client project?

choices.text: Obtain explicit written permission from the client on the exact details, or agree on an anonymised version
Publish the client's private financial spreadsheets online first and ask for forgiveness later
Invent fictional savings numbers so the case study looks more impressive to strangers
Wait ten years until the client company has closed down before mentioning the work

questions.explanation: Getting clear written approval on every published detail respects confidentiality and turns real results into trustworthy marketing.
